# A Conspiracy Of Credit Master Class: Part 2

First listed: 2026-05-14 | Evaluation cutoff: 2026-11-10

[Back to library](../README.md)

## Source versions

- [Substack: A Conspiracy Of Credit Master Class: Part 2](https://realeismanplaybook.substack.com/p/a-conspiracy-of-credit-master-class) - 2026-05-14

Earliest listed publication among matched versions, not proof of an unedited contemporaneous archive. Claim timestamps refer to the reviewed version.

## Summary

Eisman introduces bond contracts, yields, duration, taxation, ratings, credit analysis and amortization while warning about private-credit leverage and insurer connections. Several basic relationships are useful, but two central teaching claims fail: the five-year bond example confuses current yield with yield to maturity, and ratings do not mechanically set bond prices or equalize all same-rated yields. His four-C framework and acknowledgement of investors anticipating downgrades restore some missing judgment. Private-credit opacity has official support, while the scale and timing of eventual losses remain unresolved.

The lecture contains a material mathematical error and an overstated ratings-driven pricing model, rather than merely harmless terminology slips. The correct inverse price-yield relationship survives the incorrect numerical example. Distinguish conditional systemic-risk concerns from completed forecasts and unregulated from less prudentially regulated.

<a id="substack-202846896-c018"></a>
### 018. A $1,000 par bond with a 10% annual coupon pays $100 yearly; a floating coupon instead changes with its contractual reference.

**Right** | Steve Eisman | analytical principle | major

[Source at 9:38-10:10](https://realeismanplaybook.substack.com/p/a-conspiracy-of-credit-master-class) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

The arithmetic and fixed-versus-variable distinction are valid.

Conditional reasoning: Annual coupon cash flow equals stated rate times face value: 0.10 times 1,000 equals 100. A variable-rate contract substitutes the reset rate for that period.

Assessment test: Specify reset terms and payment frequency.


<a id="substack-202846896-c019"></a>
### 019. Receiving the same nominal principal decades later may leave the lender with less purchasing power.

**Right** | Steve Eisman | analytical principle | major

[Source at 9:30-9:37](https://realeismanplaybook.substack.com/p/a-conspiracy-of-credit-master-class) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

The conclusion follows when the price level rises.

Conditional reasoning: If the price index rises from P0 to PT, principal F buys F/PT units at maturity versus F/P0 initially. For PT greater than P0, purchasing power falls.

Assessment test: Compare nominal cash flows with the cumulative price index.

<a id="substack-202846896-c024"></a>
### 024. Bonds are valued objectively by mathematics rather than stories and subjective expectations.

**Wrong** | Steve Eisman | explanation | major

[Source at 11:49-12:05](https://realeismanplaybook.substack.com/p/a-conspiracy-of-credit-master-class) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

Discounted cash-flow arithmetic requires judgments about discount rates, defaults, recoveries and liquidity. Ratings are not the only subjective input.

Conditional reasoning: Price equals the sum of expected discounted cash flows. Changing an assumed default probability or discount rate changes price while leaving the formula identical; the formula therefore cannot make the inputs objective.

Assessment test: Separate the valuation identity from estimation of its inputs.

- [ABCs of credit ratings](https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/general-resources/news-alerts/alerts-bulletins/investor-bulletins/updated-8) (2017-10-12): Ratings are opinions of relative credit risk, not price determinations. They omit market and liquidity risk; methodologies and sector default experience differ, and even AAA can default.

<a id="substack-202846896-c027"></a>
### 027. For a fixed set of promised cash flows, bond prices fall when the required yield rises and rise when it falls.

**Right** | Steve Eisman | analytical principle | major

[Source at 12:36-12:50](https://realeismanplaybook.substack.com/p/a-conspiracy-of-credit-master-class) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

The inverse relationship is valid with fixed cash flows and a common discount-yield change.

Conditional reasoning: P(y)=sum(CFt/(1+y)^t). For positive fixed cash flows and y greater than -1, dP/dy=-sum(t*CFt/(1+y)^(t+1)) is negative.

Assessment test: Hold default assumptions and embedded options constant.

- [Understanding bond yield and return](https://www.finra.org/investors/insights/bond-yield-return) (2022-08-11): Current yield divides annual coupon by market price; yield to maturity discounts all remaining coupons and principal. A typical yield curve slopes upward.

<a id="substack-202846896-c028"></a>
### 028. A five-year $1,000 bond paying $50 annually must rise to $1,250 when comparable yield falls from 5% to 4%.

**Wrong** | Steve Eisman | analytical principle | major

[Source at 12:54-13:53](https://realeismanplaybook.substack.com/p/a-conspiracy-of-credit-master-class) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

This confuses current yield with yield to maturity and omits the $250 loss between purchase price and $1,000 redemption.

Conditional reasoning: Assume annual coupons, five full years remaining, no default or options, and 4% annual yield. Price=sum(t=1..5,50/1.04^t)+1000/1.04^5=1044.518223. 50/1250=4% is only current yield; a perpetual $50 stream would justify $1,250, but the stated five-year bond does not.

Assessment test: Discount all five coupons plus redemption at 4%.

- [Understanding bond yield and return](https://www.finra.org/investors/insights/bond-yield-return) (2022-08-11): Current yield divides annual coupon by market price; yield to maturity discounts all remaining coupons and principal. A typical yield curve slopes upward.

<a id="substack-202846896-c034"></a>
### 034. If recession fears drive long-bond purchases while short rates stay high, long yields may fall below short yields.

**Right** | Steve Eisman | analytical principle | major

[Source at 16:08-16:43](https://realeismanplaybook.substack.com/p/a-conspiracy-of-credit-master-class) | Stance: conditional | Horizon: not stated

This conditional price-yield mechanism follows if demand raises long-bond prices enough.

Conditional reasoning: With fixed long-bond cash flows, rising price lowers yield. If its resulting yield falls below a held-fixed short rate, the curve is inverted by definition. The condition does not identify the actual cause of every inversion.

Assessment test: Test demand, expected policy and term-premium contributions.

### 040. A rating denotes default probability, and default sends the issuer into bankruptcy court.

**Mixed** | Steve Eisman | explanation | major

[Source at 19:04-19:16](https://realeismanplaybook.substack.com/p/a-conspiracy-of-credit-master-class) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

Ratings convey relative credit risk, sometimes expected loss; failure to pay is default without logically requiring bankruptcy proceedings.

Conditional reasoning: A payment obligation can be missed before any court petition is filed. Therefore nonpayment alone is sufficient for a payment default but does not entail the separate legal act of filing bankruptcy.

Assessment test: Separate missed payments, distressed exchanges, out-of-court workouts and bankruptcy.

<a id="substack-202846896-c043"></a>
### 043. Three same-duration AA bonds issued on the same day should pay exactly the same yield regardless of industry.

**Wrong** | Steve Eisman | explanation | major

[Source at 20:01-20:42](https://realeismanplaybook.substack.com/p/a-conspiracy-of-credit-master-class) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

Equal broad credit ratings do not equal identical liquidity, recovery, covenants, tax or embedded options.

Conditional reasoning: For two bonds with equal rating and maturity, let one allow early redemption at par and the other not. Their future cash-flow sets differ when rates fall. A common rating and maturity therefore do not imply identical value or yield.

Assessment test: Compare bond-specific cash flows and market spreads.

<a id="substack-202846896-c052"></a>
### 052. A five-year $1,000 bond with a 7% annual coupon pays $70 yearly and repays principal at the end if it is a bullet bond.

**Right** | Steve Eisman | analytical principle | major

[Source at 24:48-24:59](https://realeismanplaybook.substack.com/p/a-conspiracy-of-credit-master-class) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

The cash-flow arithmetic is valid under the stated structure and successful repayment.

Conditional reasoning: 0.07 times 1,000 equals 70. Under a bullet contract, scheduled principal is zero before year five and 1,000 in year five.

Assessment test: Check call, default and amortization terms.


<a id="substack-202846896-c053"></a>
### 053. A conventional amortizing residential mortgage repays principal gradually alongside interest until the loan balance reaches zero.

**Right** | Steve Eisman | analytical principle | major

[Source at 25:00-25:14](https://realeismanplaybook.substack.com/p/a-conspiracy-of-credit-master-class) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

This follows from the fully amortizing payment schedule; it is not a claim about every possible mortgage structure.

Qualification: He refers to the ordinary 30-year mortgage example.

Conditional reasoning: Balance Bt=Bt-1*(1+r)-payment. A fully amortizing payment is chosen so BN=0 after N scheduled payments; each payment covers interest r*Bt-1 and reduces principal by the remainder.

Assessment test: Distinguish fully amortizing, interest-only and balloon loans.


## Framework and tools

- Read debt contracts and cash-flow timing before relying on labels.
- Separate coupon, current yield and yield to maturity.
- Treat ratings as one credit opinion rather than a price algorithm.
- Trace leverage through portfolio companies, funds and insurers.
- Assess capacity, collateral, covenants and character.
- Distinguish maturity from duration and promised from realized return.

Tools and charts discussed, not a complete visual inspection:

- Five-year 5% coupon versus 4% yield example
- Treasury yield curve and high-grade/high-yield comparisons
- Rating-symbol comparison chart
- Four Cs of credit analysis
- Bullet versus amortizing cash-flow schedules
- Federal and state/local interest-tax comparisons
